v1_defect_timecodes: Seg #03 (t=09.00s-13.50s): Internal source cut between t=10.71s and t=11.93s jumps from a hand drawing on paper to a talking-head woman speaking into a microphone.
Seg #04 (t=13.50s-19.00s): At t=14.16s-18.34s, intended 'drawing a curtain' shows an exterior architectural skyscraper spire instead of a curtain.
Seg #10 (t=43.70s-46.20s): Missing glyph boxes ('□') render between items on the Semantic Relay Audit card.
critic.largest_gap: The crucial first semantic pivot ('drawing a line' -> 'drawing a curtain') fails in Seg #03-#04: Seg #03 breaks mid-shot into a talking head, and Seg #04 shows a skyscraper spire instead of drawing a curtain.
critic.causal_hypothesis: Unverified internal source cut inside the clip window for Seg #03, OpenCLIP semantic false positive matching vertical architectural lines to 'curtain' in Seg #04, and an unsupported Unicode arrow glyph in Georgia.ttf.
critic.falsifiable_repair: Replace Seg #03 with verified cut-free map-drawing clip `c3c494ef` (0.2s-5.2s); replace Seg #04 with verified parted stage curtain clip `016b2487` (0.5s-6.0s) and curtained window `491529e4` (0.5s-5.0s); sanitize Unicode arrows (`->`) in card/HUD renderer.
critic.strength_to_preserve: The opening compass-arc drawing in Seg #02 (`7c61b8cd`), the drawer-pulling progression (`4b91a58f`, `2541b113`), the group drawing closer (`20cf914f`), and the structural return to the original compass line.

films.theorem: Make viewers discover a word's changing senses through successive visible actions, then use the discovered ambiguity to change the sequence's emotional direction. The first pass displays no organizing word.
films.boundary: No adjacent sources are presented as a documented encounter between their participants. First pass omits the organizing word ('draw') so the semantic relay is discovered visually before the annotated audit.

films.proof: Make a 45–60-second film organized around 'draw' using newly filmed actions or authorized source excerpts. Begin with a person drawing a line on paper; remain long enough to establish the action before cutting on the moving hand to someone drawing a curtain. Carry the curtain's scrape into a drawer being pulled open, then change scale to a group drawing closer to inspect an object. Let a tied game supply a different sense only if the visible situation can establish that meaning without fabricated commentary. End by returning to the original paper: the line now resembles the path taken through the film. Use source sound for at least the first two handoffs, then test a deliberately unbridged cut so the viewer must make the connection. Do not force every proposed sense into the proof. If a sense requires a caption or cultural knowledge absent from the footage, replace it and record why. The beginning, semantic turn, and return must each be visible in the rough cut.

films.scope: Published Sonnet critic record. Frame sheets and sound levels; no listening or normal-speed screening was reported.
films.criticText: Critic round Written by a separate agent that read frame sheets, cut lengths and sound levels. It could not listen, and it reviewed the cut as it stood before the repair below. 055 Words: Polysemic Relay. PASS (qualified) Observations I worked out the word "draw" by about 22 s without any text. 0–3.5 pencil on a map (inscribe) 3.5–6.75 film pulled off a reel (pull out) 6.75–12.9 cards drawn at a café table 13.0–22.1 a draw on a cigarette (the inhale is visible 14.5–17.5) 22.2–25.5 particle between N and S magnet blocks (attract) 25.6–31.5 a crowd, then 31.6–39.0 a statue hauled on a cable (draw a crowd / draw up) 39.0–43.4 a whiteboard diagram being drawn 43.5–46 the map pencil returns Transitions follow the sense, not the shape. The magnet cut at 22.2 is the real pivot from hand-pulling to force-pulling. Sound, measured: Audio exists only at 0–1 s, 3.5–6.7 s (about −56 dB, barely audible) and 13–21.5 s (about −33 dB). 22.2 s to the end (27 s) is digital silence . Sound stops supporting inference exactly where the film turns. At 18.5–21.5 the smoker's lips move under audio with formant-like structure. There are no captions. It may be music, as the builder says, but this needs an ear check. Largest gap: The emotional turn and the return do not land. The whiteboard diagram (39–43.4) reads as a classroom and deflates the crowd and statue section. The return to the map at 43.5 reads as "the same shot again", not as a changed meaning. Repair (falsifiable): Cut the whiteboard (39.0–43.4) and go straight from the statue on its cable (end about 38.5) to the map pencil. Prediction: a viewer asked "what is the pencil doing in the last shot?" answers something like "drawing a line / border / route", not "sketching". If they still say "sketching", the return needs a different final image. Strength to protect: the cigarette "draw" (13–22), the only shot where sound and the sense meet, and the unexplained, unbridged magnet pivot at 22.2. Ethics: The crowd and the statue come from the same source (5524afe5, per the EDL), so their adjacency does not invent an encounter. The statue removal (1921) is civic and political. It is fine as used, but it should not be pushed further toward celebration or mockery. Builder claims I disagree with: NOTES says that after the turn come "forces that pull things and people … and an emergency flight path". The whiteboard does not read as an emergency flight path. It reads as a lecture diagram. NOTES says the return makes the pencil line "read as a planned route". I did not perceive that. NOTES says captions are moot because no speech is audible. That is unverified for 13–21.5. The 055-alt "curtain" pivot (22–30 in the alt) is at least as legible as the magnet, despite NOTES saying no drawn curtain exists. It shows a curtain in motion beside a lamp. Repair after this round Whiteboard shot removed. The statue now cuts straight back to the opening map.

films.title: HOMONYM
films.description: A hand draws a line on a sheet, then a hand draws a tree. A rabbit stretches at a curtain as a narrator says 'draw'. A woman draws a curtain, a hand draws a pen out of a drawer, water is drawn from a well, a line is drawn across a map, spectators are drawn to a hall, a will is read in a drawing room. The film ends on the first hand: the line gets a dot.

films.criticText: VERDICT: inconclusive, leaning reference stronger. Cannot hear the film, so the sound-based criteria go unjudged. Noticed before the brief: at 00:17.9-21.8 the voice says "a place for everything and everything should be in its place" over hands sorting a pen tray. This is the one cut where picture and line interlock. Before that, I read the opening as "draw" (hand sketching, "draw the picture"), then "drawn" by 24.8 (map line) and 29.1 ("draw people here"), then "drawing room" at 42.8. I took the word to be "draw" and the film to be an inventory of its senses. Largest gap: the senses are listed, not relayed. Each is a new shot with a new line, and there is no action that carries a sense across a cut. Stakes and tone never change. The "will" and candle section (34-50) reads as a separate dramatic scene that does not grow out of the earlier senses. Repairs: 1. 29.1-34.0 and 42.2-49.3: the same footage runs on for about 5s each (the rows of near-identical frames). Cut each to under 2.5s, or the relay stalls. Check: no frame repeats across more than 3 consecutive sheet cells. 2. 50.7-56.3: the return does recast the opening. The rabbit appears at 50.5 on "What is it?", then the hand draws the line at 51.6-52.8 and a dot lands at 52.8. But the panda at 54.0 is a non sequitur. End on the drawing. Check: the last 3s contain no new source. 3. 24.6-34.0: three consecutive geography and tourism shots (map, hall, crowd) carry the same literal "draw". Drop one. Check: no more than two shots in a row carry the same sense. Strength to protect: the 51.6-52.8 return, where the line gets a dot and reads as a question mark.

films.scope: Published Opus blind critic record. Frames and transcripts only; sound remains unjudged until a person listens.
films.criticText: VERDICT: inconclusive, leaning reference stronger. I can't hear the film, so the sound-space criterion is unjudged. Noticed before the brief: at 0:03-0:11 a man bends to arrange theatre chairs while a woman's hands tilt and then sit on a swivel chair. The two are cut in alternating one-second steps. Both are "preparing a seat", and the narration ("chair should have a firm back support", 0:00-0:05) rhymes with both. That alignment is clear and earned. Largest gap: the film never reaches the "different outcome" it was built for. The 0:17-0:34 pairs are Iraq 1951 crouching on straw / kitchen, then sweeping / sweeping. All of it is cut at a steady one-second alternation, so the mismatch doesn't register as a mismatch. There is no wider context shot (the brief's "restore a wider view") and no final hold. The last frames (0:32-0:34) just keep cutting between brooms, so the ending feels the same as the opening. The people are not set apart as particular lives. The 1957 magenta clip at 0:29 and 0:31 reads as glitch, not information. At 34 seconds, the film is far short of the 90-second target. The small caption text is unreadable at this size, so the date states cannot be judged. Repairs: 1. 0:12-0:16: one side drops to a black or empty frame (0:15, 0:16) while the other holds. Condition: replace it with a shot of the person finishing or waiting. 2. 0:29-0:31: the 1957 pink clip. Condition: either it carries a legible date and place card, or it is cut. 3. 0:32-0:34: end on a single held wide frame of one pair for 3 seconds or more. Condition: the shot ends the cutting rhythm that came before it. Strength to protect: the chair pair at 0:03-0:11, where the cuts, the narration and the gesture all agree.

films.criticText: Critic round Written by a separate agent that read frame sheets, cut lengths and sound levels. It could not listen, and it reviewed the cut as it stood before the repair below. 057 Moments: Micro-event attention. INCONCLUSIVE Observations 0–8.4 is three near-static inserts of skates on ice. A full-resolution check found no legible change. The film opens on an inventory of picturesque fragments, which is exactly what the theorem rules out. Real micro-events, each with a beginning, change and aftermath: 8.5–12: a hand drops a tablet into a beaker and the water clouds. 12–17: a toddler pushes a door, turns, and holds an aftermath stare at the camera, 14–17. 35–38.4: a pinch of skin is released and slowly recovers. 41.6–48.5: a girl and then a boy leave through a doorway, and the empty lamp-lit room is held 46.25–48.5 . This is the one aftermath that feels necessary. Doorknob, 17–28: about 8 s of a motionless hand, then a wipe at 25.25–26.5 reveals a gleaming knob, held for only 1.25 s. The deliberate long hold comes before the change. It builds anticipation, but it is not a held aftermath. The return to the beaker (48.5–49.75) does call up the first event, but only for 1.25 s, and it fades out. Sound is almost absent: digital silence except −55 dB hiss under the toddler, about −45 dB under the bread, and about −40 dB under the beaker return. Oddly, the first beaker event (8.5–12) is silent while its return has sound. Largest gap: The opening 8.4 s teaches the wrong unit. It is a fragment, not an event. Because of that, the 8 s knob hold reads as more stillness instead of attention that has been sharpened. Repair (falsifiable): Remove the skates (0–8.4) so the film opens on the tablet drop. Prediction: viewers asked "what changed in the first shot?" all answer, and during the knob hold they say they were waiting for something to happen, not that it was "slow". Strength to protect: the empty-room hold at 46.25–48.5, and the toddler's backward stare at 14–17. Ethics: None, apart from the general care owed to footage of identifiable children. Builder claims I disagree with: The table entry "a hand works the strap (≈3.5–4.5 s)" describes a change I could not see even at full resolution. That shot does not deliver an event. Repair after this round Open. The critic advises cutting the opening skate shots, which show no change.

films.scope: Published Opus blind critic record. Frames and transcripts only; sound remains unjudged until a person listens.
films.criticText: VERDICT: inconclusive, leaning reference stronger. I can't hear the film, so I couldn't judge the room-sound rhythm. Before the brief: at 0-10s a man in suspenders adjusts his tie (0-5s, profile; 6-10s, frontal). The collar gesture reads as complete and the repetition is held. Then at 11-15s a woman cries into her fist, with the voice asking "Isn't there a better way to manage ourselves?" at 12.4s. That line pins an emotional meaning on a gesture, which is the opposite of the film's stated intent. The film looks like a montage of period-instruction footage, narrated by one lecturing voice. Largest gap: no memory-activating return. The sheet shows no return to the striped-wall setting after 10s. It ends on a standing man (44-47s) that has not appeared before, and the 43.1s line "It's worth a try" closes the film on a moral. The brief's 75s was not met either; the sheet runs 48s. Repairs: 1. Add the return to the striped wall (0-10s) after the last gesture, at about 40-48s, with the man absent or his tie finished. Check that the same frame reappears after the 38s shot. 2. Cut or move the 12.4-15.1s line over the woman. Check that 11-15s has no speech. 3. The wristwatch (18-19s) is a 2s hold on an object with no visible outcome. Extend it with the next gesture's start, or cut to 20s with the driver's head turn. Check that something changes across the cut. Strength to protect: the 0-10s collar adjustment. It is long and complete, and the profile-to-frontal shift stays specific without music.

films.proof: Make a 45-second chain using recordings supplied with suitable permission or original performances clearly identified as such. Start with one person trying to contain a laugh, retaining the quiet breath before it escapes. Cut after the first recovery to a different setting where another laugh has a contrasting rhythm. Establish at least three separate locations before any overlapping audio suggests a chorus. In the middle, let short laugh pulses overlap while the pictures remain successive, then abruptly give one participant the full duration of their recovery. End with a setting in which people have stopped laughing but are still reacting to one another; if no such authorized moment exists, end on an empty room tone rather than a fabricated reaction. Keep a separate original-context reel for review. The sound design should include breath and pauses, not just loud peaks. Compare one cut with music and one using voices alone; adopt music only if it creates an additional relation instead of instructing the audience to be happy.

films.criticText: Critic round Written by a separate agent that read frame sheets, cut lengths and sound levels. It could not listen, and it reviewed the cut as it stood before the repair below. 058 Laughs: Audible contagion. INCONCLUSIVE, leaning fail on the core (acoustic) clause Observations The separate source situations are clearly established: 0–5.6 a boy at a window smiles and withdraws 6–8.6 a man in a car throws his head back laughing 8.75–11.6 a stage comic with a tankard and chorus 11.75–16.7 children on a ride 16.75–19.2 a street 19.25–25.1 colour portraits 25.2–31.2 a group of laughing girls 32.2–38.75 boys in suits The acoustic chain, measured: Voice-band energy exists only in three blocks with hard edges: 11.75–16.75, 19.25–25.15 and 32.2–39. The two most intense visible laughs, the car man (−66 dB) and the girls (−55 dB, hiss only), are mute. The block edges are vertical in the spectrogram. There are no overlap windows, so onset → overlap → recovery never develops. There is no clipping (peak −13.7 dBFS). Montage-created exchange, not marked: the car man's laugh at 7–8.6 cuts directly to the stage comic at 8.75. These are different sources (fb5bfa37 and c6291759), and the cut reads as audience and performer. That may be intended, but nothing helps the viewer tell this cross-source exchange apart from the girls' shared in-source laughter. The grey frame at 31.2–32.2 is source runout. It reads as a dropout, not as a designed rest. Largest gap: There is no audible laughter chain. The film is a visual chain of grins over intermittent beds, so the theorem's acoustic spread is not demonstrated. Repair (falsifiable): Let the 19.25–25.15 voice block decay over 2 s into the girls' shot (25.15–27.5) at falling gain, and pre-lap the boys' room 1 s before 32.2. Prediction: the spectrogram shows overlap at 25–27.5 and 31–32.2, and a listener says the girls "pick up" the previous laughter while still being able to say it came from a different place. If they cannot tell, that is the theorem's distinction failing and has to be undone. Strength to protect: the girls' sequence (25.2–31.2) is real shared in-source laughter with physical contagion (leaning, grabbing). It is the best evidence in the batch for "people laughing together". Ethics, needs review: The film ends on the boys' scene with a heavy-set boy, head lowered and smiling uneasily (37–38.75), while others laugh around him. The relation exists in the source; the context reel shows school-dance egging-on. Ending on him isolates him as the butt of the joke. The builder's own flag also stands: the man shielding his face (16.75–19.2) sits next to unrelated laughter. The stage comic comes from a 1939 Amsterdam Jewish community film (per NOTES). Cutting a stranger's laugh "at" him (7–8.75) puts the comic in the role of the person laughed at, in a historically sensitive source. I would cut it. Builder claims I disagree with: NOTES says "the runout grey … serves as the 'empty room tone' beat". It reads as a technical dropout. NOTES says the ending shows "boys still smiling in conversation". The last 1.5 s reads as group laughter around one boy. NOTES says "no laugh sound is placed under any other person". That is true for audio, but the picture cut at 8.75 still implies a reaction across sources. Repair after this round Grey run-out frame and the closing shot of the boys removed (it singled out one boy amid group laughter); the film ends on black. The cut from the man in the car to the stage performer, and the man covering his face, are still open for a human reviewer.

films.criticText: Critic round Written by a separate agent that read frame sheets, cut lengths and sound levels. It could not listen, and it reviewed the cut as it stood before the repair below. 059 Ball: Graphic constancy. PASS (strongest proof in the batch) Observations From 0 to 17.5 the circle stays perceptually locked through sun → earth (3.5) → magnifier over a map (5.75) → magnifier over a document (8) → magnifier over an eye (10.25) → clock (12.75) → BORON dial (15.25) → octagonal meter (17.5–20.2). The octagon is the irregular object, left uncorrected, and it adds tension. Against 059-ball-control the difference is obvious: the control's magnifier sits upper-left (6–7), the shower rose sits on the left edge (24), and the motorcycle wheel is large and lower-left (31–33). Contextual release at 20.25–23.7: a wide lab shot, then a hand turning a control knob among the gauges, then the operator's face. The dials are recast as instruments of control. The score withholds its pulses here: digital silence 20.2–23.7, measured. The exit is clear. The planet drifts out of frame left (36.5–37.75), leaving stars and a passing satellite (39.75). The anchor literally leaves. Sound is a synthetic tap score whose timbre changes by section (low thumps, then about 2.5–4 kHz pings, then lower triads, then broadband clicks), in the spectrogram only. Largest gap: After the release, the second half (23.75–35.5: shower rose, speaker grille, reel, wheel, engine) goes back to plain matching. Meaning drifts but does not become more unstable, and there is no second release. Craft faults: the jet-engine source's own page-turn effect is visible at 35.25–35.5 as a squeezed frame that reads as a render error, and the end credit line is clipped at both edges (40.25–43, "…ifteen round things … 1929–200…"). Repair (falsifiable): End the engine shot at 35.2, before the source effect, and cut straight to the planet. Re-set the credit to fit the frame. Prediction: no frame between 35.0 and 36.0 shows a non-uniform transform. For meaning, a separate v2 test: widen the engine shot to show the aircraft and the person in red as a second release, and see whether viewers describe a change of scale or purpose there. Strength to protect: registration that holds through the opening, the uncorrected octagon, and the silent release. Ethics: none. Builder claims I disagree with: none of substance. Repair after this round Jet-intake shot now ends before the source film’s own page-turn effect; end-card text shortened so it is no longer clipped.

films.theorem: Show how a person's apparent social position changes when the surrounding responses become visible. Make the audience reconsider a label through observable conduct rather than invented motives.
films.boundary: Constructed from coherent multi-person table recordings (`Working Together`, 1951 and `How Quiet Helps at School`, 1953) by comparing tight isolation crops against wide room geometry of the exact same scene.
films.lineage: Lineage: Everynone / Daniel Mercadante, Losers
films.proof: Produce a 60–75-second scene with consenting adult performers, clearly presented as staged, unless a suitably authorized documentary sequence already supplies all the necessary relations. At a shared worktable, one person attempts to place a chair into a gap. Begin with a tight view of their repeated awkward adjustments so the spectator initially reads personal difficulty. Widen to show that another participant keeps moving a bag into the available space. Repeat the chair adjustment only once, now with the obstructing action visible in the same shot. A third person then moves their own chair, changing the arrangement without a speech explaining the lesson. The initially isolated person chooses a different position at the table and initiates the next shared task by passing the work to the participant who had obstructed them. End on the whole table continuing its work, with an unresolved look between two participants rather than a victorious slogan. Preserve chair scrapes, paper handling and the silence after a request. Make a comparison edit that begins wide. The critic should compare how the two openings distribute responsibility while seeing the same observed actions.

films.theorem: Make one material behavior lead to another through observable transformation: pressure, folding, wetting, adhesion, or release. Treat resemblance as a way to discover what materials can do.
films.boundary: The cut from wetted paper to dry soil/eroded rock is explicitly labeled as a visual analogy rather than a time-lapse of the same object.
films.lineage: Lineage: Provisional Operator SCION 061 · Material Affordance Chain
films.proof: Make a 50-second tabletop study with original, harmless material experiments. Begin with a dry sheet of paper held under a small weight; the sheet bends but largely returns when the weight is removed. Cut along the bending edge to a cloth taking a crease, then to a wetted paper strip that keeps a different deformation. Hold the wetting in view so the changed behavior has a visible cause. Let the dark edge of the wet area lead to an authorized close view of a weathered painted surface, but identify this as an analogy rather than a time-lapse of the same object. Return to the original dry sheet and try the first action again with the load moved. Record real contact sounds, including the quiet intervals when a surface stops moving. End with the samples side by side and their different residues visible. The film should develop a question about memory in matter without claiming that every deformation is irreversible or that the provisional reference has this structure.

films.criticText: Critic round Written by a separate agent that read frame sheets, cut lengths and sound levels. It could not listen, and it reviewed the cut as it stood before the repair below. 061 Matter: Material affordance chain. INCONCLUSIVE, with one protected-condition breach Observations There are clearly more than three material responses, each visible inside its own shot: 0–3.5 skin pinched and recovering 3.6–6.4 paper creased 6.6–9.4 foil pressed 9.6–12.4 dye plumes in water 12.6–20.3 a pour spreading into a disc, with a long satisfying hold 20.4–23.4 molten metal 23.4–32 nozzle deposits keeping their tails 32–41.4 a lathe chip curling and keeping its curl The metal → red-deposit cut did not read to me as the same material, which is good. 45.0–55.0: I read this, without notes, as real drying cracks forming after the "steam" shot at 41.5. It is in fact an animated diagram of grain growth (EDL/NOTES). Nothing on screen marks it as constructed, so a simulated response came across as observed physical behaviour. That is a direct breach of protected condition 3 and tribunal item 3. The main cut is digitally silent (−91 dB). "Sound communicates contact and recovery" fails outright. The alt-sourcesound version has long blocks with syllable-rate harmonic striations (12.9–21, 43–64), which look like narration in the spectrogram. Return at 55–58.4: the pinch is seen again after fold, set and curl. Recovery against permanence works as an idea. The 6-up comparison grid at 58.6–61.6 spells it out and weakens it. Largest gap: Sound is absent, and the grain diagram passes for footage. Repair (falsifiable): Put a visible marker on 45.0–55.0, for example "diagram" burned in for the first 1.5 s, or a hard frame/inset that shows it is a drawing. Alternatively, drop it and hold the lathe chip. Prediction: a naive viewer, asked whether 45–55 was filmed or drawn, says "drawn". I said "filmed". Separately, a v2 must find any non-speech contact audio, even 2–3 s under the lathe and the pour. Strength to protect: the 7.8 s pour (12.6–20.3) and the lathe-chip hold (32–41.4). Both durations are earned. Ethics: none. Note that the skin-pinch shot (1570ec0b) also appears in 057 and the smoker shot appears in 055 and 063. Reusing them across films dilutes each one. Builder claims I disagree with: NOTES says "furnace → diagram are cuts between visibly different films". The furnace and the diagram are the same source, and the cut did not read as a change of kind. It read as cause and effect in one process. Repair after this round The grain-growth animation is captioned “animated diagram, not filmed metal”.

films.criticText: Critic round Written by a separate agent that read frame sheets, cut lengths and sound levels. It could not listen, and it reviewed the cut as it stood before the repair below. 062 Colors: Chromatic chapters. PASS (qualified) Observations The chapters and their hinges: Yellow, 0–7.4: firefighters, first hosing and then watching. These are different actions in the same hue. Mixed-colour hinge at 7.5: a yellow engine swung out over teal sea. This hinge works. Teal: a cargo net hoisted (10.25) and a ship (15.5). A second hinge at 29.5: a pale crate over the teal sea against a red hull. Red/orange: bag packing (32.25), volunteers unloading a van (35.25), a red harvester (38.25). A thread of lifting and loading runs across the hues (engine, net, crate, bag, van), so each colour organises different stakes, not just different objects. The ending (41.25–47), a breakfast table, gathers every chapter colour : teal cloth, red curtain, yellow wall, blue sweater, orange fruit. That gives the colours a shared situation. Middle, 18.75–29.4: a glove under repair, a woman sniffing a foil pack, silhouettes against a blue screen. There is no dominant hue, and it reads as filler. Sound is source sound with three digital-silence holes (26.5–29.4, 32.2–35.2, 38.2–41.2). These fall mid-chapter and read as dropouts rather than structure. The breakfast audio shows speech-like striations, so stray dialogue is possible and needs an ear check. I saw no evidence of selective recolouring. The tones look natural and untouched. Largest gap: The middle 10.6 s breaks the chapter logic, and the red chapter is three thin 3 s fragments. Repair (falsifiable): Make 18.75–29.4 a single blue chapter: keep the silhouettes against blue and drop the glove and foil shots. Give the time to the red chapter. Prediction: asked to name the chapters afterwards, viewers list yellow, teal, (blue), red and then "everything at the table". Today I would expect most to stall at the middle. Strength to protect: the two mixed-colour hinges (7.5 and 29.5) and the breakfast-table ending. Ethics: Wildfire crew footage is fine as used. Volunteers at a van: no issue. Builder claims I disagree with: none major. I agree with the builder that the red chapter is thin. Repair after this round Open. The critic advises one blue middle chapter and more time for red.

films.theorem: Make an invisible action legible through its effects on surfaces, objects, and other actions, then shape a film's duration around unequal expansion and release.

films.proof: Build a 50–65-second film with original ordinary actions or suitably authorized material. Begin with a person gently clearing dust from a small object, showing both the breath and displaced particles without requiring a dangerous substance. Move to a light paper strip shifting near a person's mouth, then to condensation appearing on a cool transparent surface. Hold long enough for the mark to begin fading. Introduce a small mechanical fan moving a similar strip, showing the fan before making a shape match so the film does not claim the same cause. Stop the fan and let the strip settle. Return to the cooling surface as the last visible trace disappears. Use each scene's actual sound, allowing breathing to be audible where the recording supports it and leaving some effects nearly silent. Compose the sequence around unequal expansions and recoveries; do not quantize every person to one respiratory tempo. The ending should make an absence of movement perceptible through the established causes.

films.criticText: Critic round Written by a separate agent that read frame sheets, cut lengths and sound levels. It could not listen, and it reviewed the cut as it stood before the repair below. 063 Breath: Invisible force, visible consequence. FAIL Observations Human breath appears only with faces: a smoker lighting up (0–3.6; no exhaled plume visible at 4 fps) and a singer or speaker in close-up (4.75–14). Everything without a face is wind, steam or mist: a dust storm projected behind the singer (14–19.2) a sand yacht's sail (19.25–26.9) a furnace or flame (27–30) a steam jet (30–39) a steam plume (39.25–43.6) valley mist (44.5–53) Without the title I would describe the film as "air / vapour / weather", not breath. The theorem's core ("notice breath without every shot needing a face") is not achieved. There is no perceptible comparison between human and mechanical air, only a sequence of one block after the other. Sound: source voice at 4.75–19.2 only, then 38 s of digital silence (19.3–57) . That is one long dropout, not quiet intervals in a rhythm. Black holds at 3.75–4.6 and 43.75–44.4 are the only designed rests. The expansion and release shape does exist: the steam jet holds 9 s, then the plume breaks up, then the mist settles. Largest gap: There is no faceless trace of human breath, so "breath" never becomes legible through its consequences. Repair (falsifiable): Shorten the talking head (4.65–14.0) to at most 3 s. Immediately before the steam jet at 29.9, insert a faceless human exhale (a smoke plume leaving frame, or visible breath in cold air). Prediction: viewers shown the film without its title name "breath / breathing" rather than "wind / steam". Strength to protect: the 9 s steam-jet hold (30–39) and the closing mist. As release imagery they are beautiful. Ethics: none. Builder claims I disagree with: NOTES says the mechanical comparison works "structurally (separate block…)". A separate block is not a comparison the viewer feels. NOTES calls the 38 s silence "purposeful". As measured, it is one undifferentiated block. Its makeup also does not match the EDL: it marks audio on for the steam (29.9) and the mist (44.4) shots, yet both render silent, presumably because those sources have no track. The ledger should say so. Repair after this round Open. Needs a breath seen without a face; none exists in the stored footage, so v2 waits for live archive search.

films.theorem: Use repeated curves to let viewers notice a geometric relation, then make differing causes and imperfect fits part of the film's discovery. A measured resemblance remains open to correction by the object.
films.boundary: All three physical curves are seen cleanly in context before fitted hypothesis guides are overlaid. One guide visibly departs from the hand-bent strip.
films.lineage: Lineage: Will Hoffman & Derek Paul Boyle, Parabolas (etc.) (2009)
films.proof: Make a 60-second passage using three original observations: a hanging flexible chain, a small safe tossed object, and a bent strip held by a hand. Begin with the chain in context, then move closer to its profile. Cut on that profile to part of the object's flight, allowing its trajectory to unfold instead of drawing a preconceived arc. Give the hand-bent strip a slower introduction and reveal its supports. Only after all three have been seen, replay short portions with restrained, differently colored guides identified as fitted hypotheses. Let one guide visibly depart from the source so the failure becomes a useful event. End with all guides removed and a return to the chain being gently released. Record the object's contact and the strip's handling; use these events to organize rhythm rather than a voice declaring that nature follows one formula. Keep camera positions documented, since projection can change apparent curvature. The proof should remain watchable before the explanatory comparison.

films.criticText: Critic round Written by a separate agent that read frame sheets, cut lengths and sound levels. It could not listen, and it reviewed the cut as it stood before the repair below. 064 Parabolas etc.: Curves with different causes. PASS (most complete realisation in the batch) Observations The unannotated first pass (0–34.4) sets up the family resemblance before any overlay: 0–7.4 a sagging washing line 7.5–11.4 rows of laundry 12.5–14.6 a pool dive 14.75–18.4 a somersault off a platform 18.5–25.5 a swan dive from a tower with the camera panning 25.75–27.6 a hose jet 27.75–31.4 a station arch 31.5–34.4 museum arches The annotated pass (34.5–46) makes the competing causes visible: Model A: the pool dive with pan removed, where the guide fits. Model B: the tower dive with the camera moving, rms 10.6 px. The orange screen track is jagged because of camera motion. The mismatch teaches that image trajectory is not body trajectory, and it does not look like a render error. Model C: the arch, parabola rms 4.0 px against circle rms 0.42 px. It is a circle, not a parabola, with the excluded jamb points marked ×. This directly honours "do not label every curved object a parabola". The film ends on the unannotated washing line (46–50.5). That is a curve of a third cause, hanging, and it gains interest from the comparison. Sound, measured, sits only at impacts: the splash (12.5–14.6), the hose (25–27.6) and the splash again (34.4–36). That is economical and causally tied. Largest gap: The overlay labels are about 10 px on a 640×480 frame. They are readable full-size but not on a phone, and they carry most of the argument. The hose jet (25.75–27.6) reads as a straight line at this scale, the weakest member. The station arch and the museum arch are redundant. The final washing line's cause, a catenary rather than gravity on a projectile, stays invisible to anyone who does not already know it. Repair (falsifiable): Double the label size and hold each annotated model at least 3 s. Prediction: viewing on a phone, a viewer can repeat "circle fits the arch better than parabola" after one viewing. Today I predict they cannot. Also cut the station arch (27.75–31.4). Strength to protect: The order: clean resemblance first, models second, unannotated return last. Model B's honest misfit. The 4.0 against 0.42 px arch comparison. Ethics: none. The museum shot's orange/blue look should be confirmed as source tint (it is not a protected condition here). Builder claims I disagree with: NOTES says there is "no clean hanging chain … so the catenary/parabola question … is not tested". The film nevertheless opens and closes on a hanging line, so it raises the question visually. That is a strength the builder undersells, but it is fair that it remains untested. Repair after this round Open. The critic advises larger labels and a hold of at least three seconds on each fitted model.

films.description: A morning assembled from five films: a woman lays a table, a blind rises in Berlin, a woman at a sink, women washing in a river, a Dutch colonial washing channel and carriers. Each has its year or place on screen, and the film closes on a card saying it is not one morning.

shots.title: Modesta

shots.title: Indisch allerlei

films.scope: Published Opus blind critic record. Frames and transcripts only; sound remains unjudged until a person listens.
films.criticText: VERDICT: inconclusive, leaning reference stronger. I can't hear the film. Loudness and speech are the only audio evidence, and the speech is partly suspect. Noticed before the brief: 00:12.6-15.4 shows a cupboard shutter rising to reveal a ruched curtain. It is a clean, specific motion, but it is only decoration between two kitchen shots. At 00:25.1 a woman lifts a vessel in a small black-boxed frame, then holds on laundry at a stream (26.5-32.1). That is the strongest handoff. It sits next to "Oh, my God" at 27.6-31.2, which is possibly a false transcription. Largest gap: the brief asks for five distinguishable participants, and the sheet shows only about three. Two are the same American kitchen woman, and the rest are washing, carrying and coconut-hauling extras with no identification. Sepia and b/w stock changes carry the difference. Nothing visible signals "editorial construction". The English dialogue at 16-20 and 58-62 belongs to the kitchen footage, so it plays over the other cultures' action. Repairs: 1. Put an identity cue (a text or voice marker) on each participant in 25.1-32.1, 33.5-40.5, 41.9-48.9 and 50.3-54.5. Check: each block carries a distinct label. 2. At 58.7-62, remove the "new clothes" line, or move it clear of the sepia material. Check: no speech overlaps footage from another source. 3. Add a visible construction title or caption between 62 and 67.1. Check: the closing text names the day as assembled. Strength to protect: the apron-back match cuts (16.8-24 into 55.9-60) and the return to the child at the table (61.5+), where the loudness lifts to about -23 dB.

critic.largest_gap: Executes Frampton's exact cyclic slot replacement grammar across triptychs and individual specimen inspections (`163bcd54` cup, `7a6ff37f` crystal, `c78ec131` flower, `6f5ff11b` glass model, `85698632` miniature monument).

films.theorem: Advance through a fixed sequence of three structural slots [A, B, C]: in each cycle, one motif retires while a new specimen enters the freed slot, allowing viewers to deduce the replacement rule from visible recurrence.
films.boundary: The cyclic replacement index (`CYCLE 1 [A,B,C] -> CYCLE 2 [B,C,D] -> CYCLE 3 [C,D,E]`) is disclosed in the HUD without turning the historical films into mere decorative tiles.
films.lineage: Lineage: Hollis Frampton, A–Z (1967–1974)
films.proof: Make a 65–80-second original film with eight invented symbol cards, explicitly a new grammar rather than a reconstruction of Frampton's alphabet. Introduce the eight symbols once with a spoken list of their names. Run repeated cycles at a fixed slot duration; initially show only cards. Replace one slot with an ordinary action, such as a hand folding cloth, then another with light moving over a wall. Keep each replacement at the same position in subsequent cycles, advancing through a continuous source action by small increments rather than picking unrelated attractive fragments. Continue until all eight slots contain images. Leave the replacement cycles silent so the visual rhythm must carry memory. In a final passage, release one complete action from its slot duration and let its original sound arrive. End when that action finishes. Render a control in which slot order changes randomly each cycle. The comparison should reveal whether the designed order was perceptible, without claiming that any specific viewer response has already been measured.

films.proof: Choose one modest documented public event, such as a station reopening, with authorized announcement audio and at least two separately situated visual records. Build a 75–90-second essay. Begin with an uninterrupted announcement and a view whose relation to the event is stated. Replay one short phrase in a visibly marked editorial loop while showing the limited fragment that the recording actually supports. Allow an interval of blank image when the announcement refers to something no available source shows. Then widen the media context: reveal material before or after the announcement, including a sponsor or routine station ident only if it belongs to the recorded source. Finish with the announcement restored to its original continuity and a later image whose date is known. The sound should move between intact broadcast texture, deliberate loop and room silence. Do not force disagreement if the sources agree; the gap may concern certainty, perspective or what each recording leaves outside its frame.

films.scope: Published Opus blind critic record. Frames and transcripts only; sound remains unjudged until a person listens.
films.criticText: VERDICT: reference stronger (inconclusive on sound; I cannot hear it). Noticed before the brief: 0:14 to 0:15 hard cut from a bright, blown-out aerial of water to a black-bordered shoreline with a dark arc across the right edge. The ASR line "the whole harbor of Valdez is sucked dry" at 14.4-17.6 lands on it, but the sheet shows tidal flats and not a harbor. The picture does not clearly back the words. The loudness spike at 14-16s supports a narration or sound event there. Largest gap: the brief asks for a recognizable scene to return after a held surface, and for a visible scratch or boundary to carry the viewer between fragments. The sheet shows three fragments joined by hard cuts, at 0:15 and 0:22. At 0:40 the film goes to a near-blank gray leader that holds for about 7s. The park scene from 0:22 (sepia, blurred, then dissolving into horses and carriage at 0:34-0:39) does not return, and nothing links the shots by a defect. The 0:40-0:46 blank has no readable recorded noise on the sheet. Its transcript is repeated "I can't" at near-silence, which is probably false ASR from hiss. Nothing on the sheet shows scale or handling, and no narrator separates recollection from research. The film is 47s against a 60s brief. Repairs: 1. At 0:15 and 0:22, add an overlap of at least 8 frames in which a scratch or vertical line from the outgoing shot stays visible in the incoming one. Check by frame-stepping. 2. At 0:40, return to the park or carriage image before the blank. The same shot should appear at both 0:22-0:33 and about 0:39. The blank should then fall after it. 3. At 0:33-0:39, the ghosted horse image reads as a generated extension. Label it as such, or cut it. Strength to protect: the held blank leader from 0:40 to 0:46, with its dust and scratches, reads as the film's own material.

films.proof: Make a 45–60-second fictional scene using an adult performer, an original puppet, or a clearly synthetic stand-in. A person tries to fold a blank sheet and put it away. Three invented signs appear at different edges of the table. Each has a simple audible cue and one demand: unfold, turn, repeat. Establish the first demand through action before introducing the second. As the commands accumulate, the paper's growing creases make literal repetition harder, so the body must adjust rather than perform a clean loop. Let the third sign occupy the space where the person wants to place the finished fold. End when the performer keeps the folded sheet in their hands and declines to follow the next cue; the sign continues briefly, then loses its spatial support. Record paper and bodily contact sounds, and make the absence of an expected cue a decisive event. Keep the visual vocabulary original and small enough that cause and resistance remain readable.

films.criticText: VERDICT: pass, narrowly. I can't hear the film, so voice quality and the 57.5 "Thank you" (likely hiss) are unjudged. Noticed before the brief: at 0:35-0:40 the "untouched kitchen" fills with two coated visitors seen from behind, with rope stanchions and a rail in frame. The narration at 25.9-27.5 says "Nobody had touched the kitchen." The picture undercuts the voice, so the room reads as an exhibit before any caption says so. At 48.5 the voice contradicts itself ("didn't have gloves... wasn't in a dress"), which is a real, concrete break. Largest gap: the reveal is carried by tiny, low-contrast captions at 0:58-1:13, after speech has stopped (loudness about -37 dB). It reads as a recap of earlier clips, not a discovery. The 52-57s close-ups of the boy run with no narration, so the emotional payoff is silent and unanchored. Repairs: 1. Enlarge the captions at 58.3-73.7 so they are legible at thumbnail size. Check: caption text height at least 3% of frame height. 2. Add one narrated line over 1:10.6-1:12.1, for example the narrator naming the borrowed footage, so the final 15s is not caption-only. Check: speech present in that window, loudness above -30 dB. 3. Cut the 53.7-56.8 close-ups to 2s, or put a line over them. Check: no speech gap longer than 4s between 43s and 58s. Protect: the kitchen sequence at 23-40s. The narration lists details (plant, red chair, icebox) that match the frames, and the exhibit rope then breaks the claim without any comment.

films.proof: Build a ninety-second observational passage from authorized recordings of two children investigating a familiar container, with caregivers choosing safe objects and remaining present. The first twenty seconds establish one child, the container, and the nearby adult without instructional text. Keep the hesitation before the child reaches. A hand meets a resistant lid; the child pauses and looks elsewhere. Cut to the second setting only after that pause has become legible. Here the container opens readily, but its contents are out of reach. Preserve the different problem rather than manufacturing matching success. At sixty seconds return to the first recorded session: if the child resumes, show the actual resumption; if not, allow the abandoned object to remain. End on an adult responding to whichever attempt the material genuinely contains. Let local voices, floor contact, and container sounds remain distinct. Do not use a triumphant score or accelerated montage to turn uncertain activity into an achievement race.

Open on a closed laundrette, a bakery worker moving a tray, and an early bus stop; preserve enough context to locate each activity. films.proof: Build a two-minute district symphony from authorized observation of one street over declared recording sessions. Open on a closed laundrette, a bakery worker moving a tray, and an early bus stop; preserve enough context to locate each activity. A rolling cart supplies a pulse that passes through a washing-machine drum and bicycle pedals, but let each shot reveal what the movement accomplishes. At the midpoint, refuse the growing beat: hold on a person waiting while others pass, with ordinary traffic sound replacing the score. Resume through a practical encounter, such as a delivery that briefly blocks a doorway and changes two people’s movement. End with the laundrette closing or settling into a different shift, returning to the opening frame with altered light and activity. If recordings come from multiple days, disclose the constructed day arc. An original score can gather and disperse rhythms, but never present the silent-film reference’s soundtrack as recovered location audio.

VERDICT: reference stronger (leaning inconclusive on sound; I cannot hear the film, so the "original sound phrase" and any coordination by sound go unjudged). Noticed before the brief: at 0:17-0:24 the film cuts between a log and a mallet (0:17-0:19, 0:23-0:24), the mallet worker (0:20) and the engine-block hand (0:21). Then at 0:22 it cuts back to the woman at the wheel, with the cuts landing on the narration "mallet... carpenter". It reads as one repeated beat, but the transcript's talk of tires, stools and "oil business" does not describe what the frames show (engine blocks, a furnace). That mismatch is probably recogniser error in the hiss, so I treat it as unreliable. Largest gap: the brief wants an interruption kept at normal speed, and I see none. The sheet shows only continuous labor across 44s. The "interruption" at 0:17-0:19 is a static log with no worker. It is an insert, not a maintenance interval, and it lasts about 3 seconds. The target is 90s and this is 44s. The loudness data shows nothing that reads as a coordination phrase, and a drop to -45.9 dB at 42s suggests an abrupt end. The ending at 0:42-0:43 is the mallet worker again, still working. Nothing stops, so the brief's end condition is unmet. Repairs: 1. 0:17-0:19: replace the log insert with one complete waiting or maintenance shot of 6s or more at real speed. Check that a worker is visibly idle or tending the machine. 2. 0:42-0:43: end on a stopped hand or machine. Check that the last frame shows no motion. 3. 0:25-0:35: add one wide contextual shot. Check that it shows what the close crop at 0:09-0:16 left out. Protect: the 0:36-0:41 engine-block sequence with the 0:42 return to the mallet worker. It shows a changed framing on return.

VERDICT: reference stronger (a pass is not earned). I cannot hear the film; the sound phrase and any rhythm coordination are unjudged. Speech recognition in the hiss is partly unreliable. Noticed before the brief: 17.1-18.3 is a hard cut to a static wood block on a stump. By 19.6 it returns to the mallet worker from 4.9-7.3, so the film recycles the same clips. The narration is also mismatched. "Carpenter... stool" (5.7-9.1) plays over a woman at a machine, and "tire... flipper" (9.1-17.2) plays over the same woman. The ASR lines are loose, but they do not match the pictures. Largest gap: there are no three distinct processes with an established repeated movement. Cylinder-block hands, the mallet worker, the woman at the wheel, the hard-hat worker, the machine operator and the furnace all get one or two brief appearances. No beat is visibly repeated, and no maintenance or waiting interval appears (30.5-40.3 is a continuous task). There is no return that reveals excluded framing. The ending at 54.9-57.4 is a static hand close-up, not a worker or machine stopping. Repairs: 1. Cut the sheet to three processes, with 3 or more visible repetitions each by 0-30s. Check: each process appears in at least 3 shots, with the same action visible in each. 2. Hold one maintenance or wait shot unbroken for 4s or more at normal speed, around 30.5-40.3. Check: one continuous shot with no cut and a visible pause in the work. 3. Replace 54.9-57.4 with a wider re-frame of the 4.9-7.3 mallet worker, ending on the mallet stopping. Check: the frame is wider than at 4.9 and shows the mallet at rest. Strength to protect: the high-contrast black-and-white texture and the hands-and-machinery close-ups (0-3.7, 46.4-51.3) read clearly as labor.

films.proof: Stage an original seventy-second scene at a quiet library counter. A visitor arrives carrying a damaged book and a repair slip. In close fragments, one hand places the slip under the book, another reaches for a pencil, and a third object—a small photograph used as a bookmark—slides into view. Hold the visitor’s hesitation before they cover the photograph. A clerk’s hand stops short of taking the book; a soft drawer sound suggests another task beyond the frame. Use the next transfer to change trust: the visitor deliberately separates the photograph and offers the book again. Only then reveal enough of the counter to show that the clerk has prepared a protective sleeve, not a penalty notice. End on the photograph being returned inside the sleeve and the book remaining for repair. Keep paper friction, pencil contact, and the drawer audible. No dialogue should explain the visitor’s initial fear; the action and delayed context must make the changed relation available.

films.criticText:
VERDICT: inconclusive, leaning reference stronger. The sheet is only 42s against a 52s brief. I cannot hear the film, so contact sounds are unjudged. Noticed before the brief: the bowler's back view recurs at 0-1s, 4-5s, 9-11s and 12-13s. He swings and releases at 5s and 10-11s, with cutaways to the pool diver at 2-3s and the tower diver at 6-8s. This reads as a graphic-match rhythm. The 12-13s frames show the pins and the bowler standing apart, so the pin crash never arrives. At 14-29s dives and splashes (23-25s) run together as one undifferentiated flight-and-splash stretch. Largest gap: no readable release-to-consequence structure. The brief asks for six bounded excerpts with clear outcomes. The sheet shows two cutaways to the bowler, then a long unrelated run of dives. The woman on the board (30-38s) is a nine-second static hold with no action. The ending is a hand folding cloth at 39-41s, with only garbled ASR over hiss ("the line is on the line" loops), so that line is likely false. I cannot see a consequence that changes this release's weight. Repairs: 1. Cut the 30-38s hold to at most 3s, or add a release within it. Check: no frame is held static for more than 3s. 2. Show the pins falling after the 10-11s release, at 12-13s. Check: pin motion is visible within 2s of release. 3. Reorder so the 14-25s dives repeat the pattern with a visible cut-away before the release. Check: each cut-away lands before the foot leaves the board. Strength to protect: the bowler/pool/tower alternation at 0-11s. It is legible and rhythmic.

VERDICT: reference stronger (fails the brief as it stands on the sheet). Noticed before the brief: the bowler seen from behind recurs at 0-1, 4-5, 9-11. At 5-6 and 10-11 he is already mid-release or past it, so the film cuts to the pole climber or the diver on the beat. At 12-13 the pins are already down. Pool shots at 2-3 interrupt the bowler. This reads as a rhythmic cutaway pattern, not a first-time consequence. Largest gap: the film has no visible release/consequence structure past about 13s. 14-24 is a long run of diver and fall footage with a blurred whip at 22. Then comes a demolition at 23-24 and a spray at 25-28. Those are loosely related falls, not hands letting go. The woman on the board holds a static pose for 6 seconds (29-34). That is stasis, not an earned hesitation, and the sheet shows no phase alignment. The napkin ending at 35-38 is barely an object transfer, and there are no readable hands. films.criticText: VERDICT: reference stronger (leaning inconclusive on sound; I cannot hear the film, and the transcript's "Chug"/"Little"/"Fiamco" are probably hiss false-positives). Noticed before the brief: at 0:00-0:12 a boy crosses a fixed-camera room, carries a chair to the window, climbs on it and appears to fiddle with the blinds, and leaves it tipped over at 0:11. From 0:13 to ~0:31 the room is empty and the frames are almost static. A figure flickers at 0:23 (a hat or head at the desk), a possible removal artifact. At 0:32-0:39 a split screen shows left recorded, right removed. At 0:40-0:46 a red mask appears over the figure. Largest gap: there is no cup and no routine. The brief wants an intact passage, then the same passage with the person removed while the chair movement remains. Here the person is gone from frame 0:13 on, and about 18 s of empty room follows with almost no change (loudness is flat near -18.5 dB). Nothing is established as ordinary, so no deviation can register. The film is also 46.7 s, not 60 s. Repairs: 1. Show the intact passage and the removed passage back to back, not the split screen. Check: by 0:20 the same chair movement appears with the boy visible, then without him. 2. Cut the empty hold at 0:14-0:31 to a length that has a visible event. Check: something in the room changes (chair settles, blind moves) at least every 5 s. 3. Remove the 0:23 flicker, or show it deliberately. Check: a frame-by-frame look shows no stray figure in the empty stretch. Strength to protect: the red-mask explanation at 0:40-0:46, with its caption, makes the intervention inspectable.

films.proof: Stage a ninety-second scene in a modest municipal waiting room. A clerk at a rear counter calls ticket numbers while a cleaner in the foreground tries to mop a small leak. The rule is simple: nobody may move their chair until their number is called. Establish it through one polite correction rather than an explanatory sign filling the screen. As the damp patch expands, waiting people lift their feet, tilt bags, and gradually balance in increasingly inconvenient positions without leaving their chairs. A newcomer takes a ticket and must decide where to sit. The clerk continues working sincerely, while the cleaner’s practical route is blocked by the compliant queue. Keep the camera fixed and the performances restrained; chair friction, dripping, and the ticket machine occupy different acoustic distances. Near the end the clerk calls a number belonging to an empty chair, and everyone waits for an absent person to respond. Hold long enough for the viewer to see how the room has reorganized itself around obedience, then cut before a punchline explains it.

films.proof: Stage a ninety-second scene in a modest municipal waiting room. A clerk at a rear counter calls ticket numbers while a cleaner in the foreground tries to mop a small leak. The rule is simple: nobody may move their chair until their number is called. Establish it through one polite correction rather than an explanatory sign filling the screen. As the damp patch expands, waiting people lift their feet, tilt bags, and gradually balance in increasingly inconvenient positions without leaving their chairs. A newcomer takes a ticket and must decide where to sit. The clerk continues working sincerely, while the cleaner’s practical route is blocked by the compliant queue. Keep the camera fixed and the performances restrained; chair friction, dripping, and the ticket machine occupy different acoustic distances. Near the end the clerk calls a number belonging to an empty chair, and everyone waits for an absent person to respond. Hold long enough for the viewer to see how the room has reorganized itself around obedience, then cut before a punchline explains it.

films.scope: Published Opus blind critic record. Frames and transcripts only; sound remains unjudged until a person listens.
films.criticText:
VERDICT: inconclusive, leaning reference stronger. The sheet supports only about 20s of a 90s proof, and I can't hear the film. Noticed before the brief: at 0:03-0:06 a woman sets the table while a man and a girl enter from a back doorway. By 0:11 the father is seated and the son stands at the table. The camera seems fixed with a slight drift. At 8.9-12.6 a narrator says "For once, Ma and Pa sat down to supper without being dog tired." That line explains the scene instead of letting timing carry it. Largest gap: there is no obstruction and no second activity at a different depth. The scene is one ordinary routine, a family assembling for supper. The mother walks through the frame at 0:14-0:17 and sits, which looks like ordinary blocking, not a deviation. At 0:18-0:19 the frame shows a completed arrangement, but nothing suggests a conflict. Narration also directs attention, which the primary operator forbids. Repairs: 1. Cut the voiceover line at 8.9-12.6. Condition: no narration over the held frame, and the viewer learns the "tired" premise from behavior. 2. Add a visible obstruction between 0:06 and 0:12, such as the son blocking the mother's route. Condition: one person's path visibly changes while another activity continues at a different depth. 3. Make the 0:18-0:19 state differ materially from 0:00, for example a vacated chair or an unserved plate. Condition: a frame comparison shows a change in arrangement beyond people sitting down. Strength to protect: the locked, deep kitchen composition, with the table in the foreground and the doorway behind it. It lets entrances at different depths read within one frame.

VERDICT: reference stronger (the film does not meet its brief; I could not judge sound, and the sheet shows no pass). Before the brief: I saw a locked-off view of a white clapboard building. Men with lapel rosettes come out through the door and shake hands, one pair after another. At 00:09 a large white-dot overlay sits on one man's coat. It reads as a glitch or a stamp, not as part of the action. At 00:34 a man runs across the frame with his arm out. This is a convention-style exit, charming but repetitive. Largest gap: the brief wants two activities at different depths, an obstruction that reroutes one person, and an ending that differs from the opening. The sheet shows one activity, in one plane, in a cycle that repeats from 00:00 to 00:35. Frame 00:35 is the same arrangement as 00:00. There is no second depth plane, no obstruction and no accumulating pressure. The loudness is flat at about -41 dB throughout, and the only speech is "We're here" at 0.0 and "This is the point" at 28.6. Both are probably false, and "This is the point" would be an unwanted narrator line if real. I can't hear the film, so I can't judge the sound-driven discovery the brief asks for. Repairs: 1. Remove or justify the dot overlay at 00:09. Check: no non-photographic mark in any frame from 00:00 to 00:35. 2. Delete the speech at 0.0-0.7 and 28.6-30.0. Check: no recognized words in the transcript. 3. Stage a visible obstruction by 00:15 that changes one man's route. Check: by 00:35 the door area is arranged differently from 00:00. Strength to protect: the locked camera and the rhythm of handshakes and hats at the doorway (00:12-00:19).

films.proof: Stage three original thirty-second tableaux around two volunteers trying to place a repaired chair where it is needed. In the first room, they carry it into a community hall and say, “Someone might need it.” A caretaker agrees but cannot store it, leaving the volunteers holding its weight through a polite pause. In the second room, an office already has identical empty chairs; the same phrase sounds less confident as the volunteers are asked to complete a form before setting it down. In the third, they reach a corridor where a tired cleaner is standing beside supplies. The cleaner sits before either volunteer can finish the phrase. Keep each scene in a fixed, self-contained composition. The chair develops one visible scuff, and the person bearing most of its weight changes. Let room acoustics, breaths, and contact sounds replace a continuous comedy track. End on the volunteers remaining upright with nothing left to carry, unsure whether their task is complete.

films.proof: Construct a two-minute original film around a garden workbench using authorized observation, with any human staging declared. A gardener places a cracked empty pot beside a young plant and leaves the frame. Instead of following the person, remain until an actually recorded insect or snail becomes the next focus; choose a source interval containing genuine movement rather than forcing the animal into a planned action. Its route leads attention toward the plant’s edge. A plainly marked passage of time brings a later observation of that plant moving in wind or shedding a dry leaf. The leaf lands beside the cracked pot, giving material texture a new prominence. Finish with a documented reuse of the broken pot as drainage material, or retain the unresolved fracture if no such process was recorded. Human tool sounds may disappear while air, leaf contact, and small environmental sounds remain. End on the altered arrangement of the bench, allowing the original person to remain absent. The relay should be felt through persistence in the place, not explained as a universal cycle.

films.proof: Stage an original seventy-five-second scene at an apartment building’s shared noticeboard. Begin in a centered frontal composition with three residents arriving from distinct doors to post incompatible announcements in the same empty rectangle. Their footsteps and door sounds establish a small schedule. The first person places a notice precisely; the second reaches to add another and discovers there is only one pin; the third waits holding a much larger sheet. A deliberate lateral camera move reveals a second, previously unseen board labeled for the relevant purpose, but a delivery trolley blocks access. The residents rearrange themselves through practical cooperation, temporarily breaking the opening symmetry. Keep the acting dry and the objects ordinary. Return to a frontal composition only after their routes have changed: the large sheet now covers both small notices, while the single pin remains in someone’s hand. End on the delayed sound of one more resident arriving offscreen. An original short musical phrase may establish order, then stop when cooperation replaces the schedule.

films.proof: Create a forty-five-second passage from authorized recordings of a neighborhood bakery, a bicycle workshop, and a waterside walkway, clearly credited as separate places. Begin with a hand pushing a bakery door across frame. Carry its direction into a wheel being turned at the workshop, then use the wheel’s actual rotation to lead toward a curved railing seen while the camera moves on the walkway. Do not force a precise match by deforming people or architecture. At fifteen seconds stop the acceleration with a sustained workshop view in which a mechanic waits for someone to bring a tool; its ordinary sound should expose the human interval behind the motion. Resume with three short transitions whose incoming actions begin before the outgoing momentum has fully resolved. Use an original score and actual impacts rather than the reference film’s music. End on a stationary wide view of the water, allowing one earlier mechanical sound to fall away. The final stillness should register as release, while the separate locations remain recoverable and visually distinguishable.

films.criticText: VERDICT: inconclusive, leaning reference stronger. It fails the brief on length (44.6s against 60s), and I cannot hear whether the sound bridges work. Noticed before the brief: at 0:03-0:06 the film cuts from the purple beach jogger to a grey street where a crowd runs toward camera. Direction and mood change, and that reads as a leap. At 0:12-0:18 a close-up of a USA runner (#935) stands in for the pursuit, and there are interview lines about "one event left" over it. At 0:29-0:44 a girl by a sign sits in the same sepia frame for 15 seconds. Largest gap: the ending. The brief wants someone stopping while the world keeps moving. The sheet shows a tiny figure in a static sepia frame (0:29-0:36, 0:40-0:44) and no motion around her. It is stillness with no momentum behind it, and the same shot is used twice, so it reads as a hold. The brief's "someone waiting or recovering" rest and its "resume" step are not visible. Repairs: 1. 0:40-0:44: cut it, or replace it with a shot where traffic or a crowd passes a stopped person. Check: motion is visible in the background for at least 3s. 2. 0:37-0:39: the tennis runner repeats 0:07-0:11 and the sepia shot repeats 0:29-0:36. Check: no source shot appears twice. 3. 0:12-0:18: a static close-up is not a leap of place. Check: the cut at 0:12 or 0:19 shows a different place, with the runner's direction carried across it. Strength to protect: 0:03-0:06. The crowd running toward camera is the only moment where direction transfers. Limit: I cannot hear the film, so the bridges and the local sound at 0:12-0:22 are unjudged. The "Thank you" at 30.7s is probably a false hit on hiss.

A brief original narration may state the bounded question: what does a delayed release make the other person do? The third excerpt should resist the emerging account—for example, an object is released immediately, yet obligation persists through a later response. End by returning to the first scene’s wider context rather than claiming that all hands express the same thing. films.proof: Make a ninety-second fable with one original figure and one movable object. In the first movement, hovering nearby or a touch approximation makes the figure notice the visitor; immediate repeated tapping makes its response hurried and eventually guarded. In the second, the figure offers the object only after a pause. Holding it briefly produces a sustained tone and changes the figure's posture. Pulling abruptly causes the figure to retain it; waiting allows a voluntary release. In the final movement, the visitor can return the object or remain still. Both lead to distinct, completed endings, with a clear invitation to begin again. Sound is part of turn-taking: the figure's short syllables have space for the visitor's gesture, and overlapping gestures interrupt a musical phrase rather than merely increasing volume. Provide touch, pointer and keyboard equivalents. The proof uses drawn or crafted characters and credited synthetic sound, with no claim to depict a real person's mental state.

Give the visitor three optional invitations: record an empty place for four seconds, record something moving without leaving its position, and record a hand placing an ordinary object down. films.proof: Build a ninety-second active session from twelve authorized clips, each twelve to twenty seconds long, under hold, wait and leave. Only one clip advances at a time. Selection records an opening; full normal-speed coverage records completion. Rapid clicking may open every item, so never promise unopened links. Begin calmly, multiply invitations in the middle, then reveal remaining time. Pause freezes the countdown, all media and narrative navigation; only resume or exit advances the session state. Exit stops it and opens the quiet index. At eighty active seconds, freeze the route record. The final ten seconds replay its fragments with silence and report actual opened, completed and unopened counts against twelve; this coda does not alter completion records. Offer the same untimed index afterward, with the session snapshot preserved while index exploration is tracked separately. Use original composed speech only as authored text. Keep the proof local, without personal tracking or claims about the visitor's psychological state.

films.scope: Published Opus blind critic record. Frames and transcripts only; sound remains unjudged until a person listens.
films.criticText:
VERDICT: inconclusive, leaning reference stronger. I cannot hear the film, so the sound requirement is unjudged. Noticed before the brief: at 00:20.870, 00:45.914 and 01:08.871 the picture goes black and small caption text appears ("Working history cleared (1 of 3)", and so on). The same five excerpts then return in the same order: the pencil curve, street sweeping, mallet and wedge, the empty chairs, and the mother with the toddler. The captions at 01:31–01:36 say "five of twelve excerpts, in the same order, four times. Seven were never used." Largest gap: the film shows loop, not forgetting. Four identical passes, with identical speech each time ("What are plastics?" at 0.0, 23.1, 46.9 and 70.3), mean there is no variation to compare. The brief's "intact recurrence beside a changed one" is barely visible. The only change I can see is the 01:15 street shot, which shows a different frame of the same shot. The twelve-excerpt archive is claimed in text only, since only five appear. Repairs: 1. At 01:15.132–01:36.002, the final pass must hold one excerpt unchanged and one visibly altered, with a caption naming which is which. Check by frame-diffing it against the pass at 52.175. 2. At 20.870, 45.914 and 01:08.871, each reset card should hold at least 3s and read as legible, since it is currently tiny and low-contrast. Check that the text is at least about 4% of frame height. 3. Make each pass use at least one different excerpt of the twelve, in at least 2 of the 4 passes. Check by counting unique sources, which should be above 5. Strength to protect: the black reset cards cut hard between the passes, and the identical opening line at each pass makes the return recognizable.

VERDICT: reference stronger (leaning inconclusive). I cannot hear the film; speech recognition in hiss may be false. Noticed before the brief: at 0:20.9 to 0:23.3 the screen goes black with the text "Working history cleared. (1 of 3)". After it, the same cycle restarts. The drawn curve (0:00), the street sweepers, the carpenter and the chairs return in identical order at 0:25.6, 0:48.9 and 1:14.5. The transcript repeats "What are plastics?" at 0:24, 0:49, 1:14 and 1:35. The loop reads clearly, and the black cards act as the resets. Largest gap: the changed state 4 is not legible. The final split screens (1:35 to 1:44) look nearly identical, left against right. The caption says "Clearing the history changed almost nothing", but the sheet shows no visible change to point to. Sound is also degraded and garbled by state 3 ("Retie", "come ball the brake ball"), with no sign this was meant. The film announces its finding instead of letting the viewer find it. Repairs: 1. At 1:35.4 to 1:44.8, make the left and right panels differ in one checkable way, such as the order of two shots or the cut at 1:42.4. A viewer with the sound off should be able to name the difference. 2. At 1:09.8 to 1:14.5, hold the third reset card so the transcript at 1:12 to 1:14 matches it. Condition: ASR returns "plastics" cleanly after the reset. 3. At 1:44.8 to 1:51.7, the black final card sits over silence (-91 dB from 1:46). Cut it to 3 s or add a returning sound cue. Protect: the identical black reset cards at 0:20.9, 0:46.6 and 1:09.8. They are the clearest recognition device in the film.

films.proof: Make a two-minute film about a repeated unfinished task using the operator's own expendable materials: for example, copies of abandoned drafts and one empty frame. Establish the actual condition in a held shot. The maker states a modest question rather than a promised cure, then sorts the copies into what will be kept, revised and relinquished. Film the sorting long enough for hesitation to be visible. The material action is simple and safe: fold the relinquished copies into supports for the frame, so discarded work literally holds an open space. Preserve paper sounds and room tone; music, if used, must not announce emotional resolution. Return after a short documented interval and record what the maker did or did not put in the frame. End on this observed condition. Offer a minimal index for revisiting preparation, action and aftermath, but keep the uninterrupted film as the primary work. All personal materials and testimony are voluntary and within the maker's authority.
